Topic 1: Data Structure Design & Augmentation

Background & Tricks: A major part of this course involves taking a standard data structure (like an AVL tree or a Heap) and augmenting it to support new operations in or time.

  • The "Augmentation" Trick: You can store additional fields in a tree node (like size, sum, or min) as long as the field can be computed solely from the node's children. Because AVL tree rotations only affect a constant number of nodes, updating these fields during insertions and deletions takes only time.
  • The "Global Shift" Trick: If an exam question asks you to update all elements in a structure simultaneously in time, you cannot iterate over the elements. Instead, maintain a global variable (e.g., GlobalShift). When you insert a new item , you actually insert . When you query an item, you return its stored value .

Test Questions:

  • Question 1.1: Design a data structure that contains integer keys and supports the following operations:
    1. insert(x) in time.
    2. delete(k) in time.
    3. find(k) in time.
    4. shift(d): Adds the integer to all keys currently in the data structure in time.
    5. EvenSum(): Returns the sum of all keys in the data structure that currently have an even value in time.

  • Question 1.2: Propose a data structure that supports:
    1. push(S, x): inserts into the structure in time.
    2. pop(S): removes the last inserted element in time.
    3. Reduction(S, d): reduces the value of all elements currently in by in time.
    4. Max(S): returns the maximum value in in time.

Topic 2: Dynamic Programming (DP)

Background & Tricks: Dynamic programming questions test your ability to break a problem into overlapping subproblems and define a recursive state. Your solution must always include a recursive formula, base cases, a description of the table/matrix used, and the order of filling it.

  • The State Definition Trick: The most important part of DP is defining the state or clearly. Often, should be defined as "the optimal solution for the prefix ending exactly at index ".
  • The Space Optimization Trick: Exam questions almost always ask "Can the space complexity be improved?". If your recurrence for row only depends on row or , you do not need to keep the entire matrix in memory. You only need to keep the last 1 or 2 rows, reducing space to .

Test Questions:

  • Question 2.1 (The Zig-Zag Subsequence): A sequence of numbers is called a "Zig-Zag" sequence if (strictly alternating up and down). Given an array of length , write a DP algorithm to find the length of the longest Zig-Zag subsequence. Provide the recursive formula, time complexity, and explain how to optimize the space complexity.

  • Question 2.2 (The Snake Path): Given a 2D matrix of integers, a "Snake Path" is a path starting at and moving either right or down. Furthermore, the absolute difference between any two adjacent cells on the path can be at most 1 (). Write a DP algorithm to find the longest Snake Path in the matrix.

Topic 3: Hash Tables & Expected Time

Background & Tricks: Hash tables resolve collisions using chaining or open addressing to provide average-case (expected) time for Insert, Search, and Delete.

  • The "Expected Time" Trigger: If an exam question asks you to solve an array problem in expected time ("בתוחלת"), this is a direct hint to use a Hash Table. Sorting takes , but hashing takes expected time.
  • The "Complement Search" Trick: For questions asking to find a pair of numbers satisfying an equation (like ), insert all numbers into a hash table, then iterate through the array again and search for the complement (e.g., ) in expected time per lookup.

Test Questions:

  • Question 3.1: You are receiving a stream of distinct integer keys . You are given a predetermined constant . Design a data structure that, whenever a new key arrives, answers in expected time whether there exists a previously seen key () such that .
  • Question 3.2: Given an unsorted array of numbers, where it is known that there are only distinct numbers, prove or disprove: It is possible to sort this array in expected time.

Topic 4: Disjoint Sets (Union-Find)

Background & Tricks: Disjoint Sets track a partition of elements into non-overlapping groups. Using a disjoint-set forest with Union by Rank and Path Compression yields a running time of for operations, which is asymptotically optimal and practically linear.

  • The Graph Component Trick: Union-Find is universally used for finding connected components or detecting cycles in graphs (e.g., Kruskal's algorithm).
  • The "Piggyback" Trick: If you are asked to support an operation that prints or extracts all elements of a specific set quickly, you cannot just iterate over the Union-Find tree. Instead, augment the structure by maintaining a standard Linked List for each set. When you call Union, you splice the two linked lists together in time.

Test Questions:

  • Question 4.1: You need to design a disjoint-set data structure that supports the standard MakeSet(x), Find(x), and Union(x, y) operations, but additionally supports a Print(x) operation. Print(x) must print all the elements currently in the same set as in time, where is the size of the set. Describe the structural modifications needed to support this.
  • Question 4.2: Explain how path compression works during a Find-Set(x) operation. Does path compression change the rank of the nodes? Why or why not?

Topic 5: Lower Bounds & Contradiction Proofs

Background & Tricks: You must deeply understand the fundamental limits of algorithms. The most common limit tested is that comparison-based sorting requires time in the worst case.

  • The Reduction Trick: If an exam question asks you to "Prove or Disprove" the existence of a data structure that does something suspiciously fast (like finding medians dynamically or extracting items), see if you can use it to sort an array. If the data structure could be used to sort an array in time (faster than ), the claim is false and you have your disproof.

Test Questions:

  • Question 5.1: Prove or disprove the following claim: It is possible to implement a "Median Heap" data structure that supports the following operations:
    1. Init(A): Builds the structure from an array of elements in time.
    2. Extract-Median(): Removes and returns the median of the structure in time.
    3. Return-Median(): Returns the median without deleting it in time.
  • Question 5.2: Suppose you are given sorted arrays, where the total number of elements across all arrays is . Write an algorithm to merge all arrays into a single sorted array in time. Prove why this cannot be done in time if is large.

Topic 6: Amortized Analysis

Background & Tricks: Amortized analysis proves that even if a single operation is incredibly expensive, the average cost over a sequence of operations is small.

  • The Potential Method: You define a potential function representing "stored energy." The amortized cost is defined as .
  • The Dynamic Array Trick: For arrays that double in size when full, the expensive step is copying elements. A perfect potential function is (where num is the number of elements and size is the array capacity). This ensures you build up enough "energy" to pay for the copy operation when the array overflows.

Test Questions:

  • Question 6.1: Consider a dynamic array that starts at size and is completely full. When we insert a new element, we allocate a new array of size and copy all elements over. Using the potential function , prove formally that the amortized cost of an insertion is .
  • Question 6.2: In a binary counter, incrementing the counter might require flipping multiple bits, taking up to time for a single increment. Use the Aggregate Method or Accounting Method to prove that a sequence of increments takes time overall.

How to Use This Guide:

  1. Do not look at the source materials right away. Try to draft the pseudocode, the data structure fields, and the mathematical proofs on a blank piece of paper.
  2. For the DP questions, force yourself to write out the 4 steps (State, Recurrence, Base Cases, Order of execution) strictly.
  3. For the Data Structure design questions, verify that your "Tricks" (like GlobalShift or augmented size attributes) actually run within the required Big-O bounds during tree rotations.
